The Longspined bullhead (Taurulus bubalis) exhibits several well-defined life-history thresholds that have been characterized through field studies. Mark-recapture surveys across coastal rocky habitats in the northeastern Atlantic indicate that individuals attain an ultimate total length of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters], a size typically reached after several years of steady growth. The body weight associated with this maximum size has been estimated from length-weight regressions, with the ultimate wet weight recorded at approximately 87 grams [Wwi = approximately 87 grams], a value that reflects the relatively robust, broad-headed morphology of this sculpin. Gonadal inspections from seasonal collections reveal that the onset of reproductive capability, or puberty, occurs at a considerably smaller body size; fish become sexually mature at a total length of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters]. At this maturation point, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 31 grams [Wwp = approximately 31 grams], indicating that individuals must more than double their body mass from maturity to reach their asymptotic dimensions. These size benchmarks are crucial for understanding the species' demographic structure and its response to environmental variability in temperate nearshore ecosystems.

Reproductive output in the Longspined bullhead is closely tied to the size of the female, with fecundity increasing substantially after the attainment of sexual maturity. During the spawning season, which typically occurs in late winter to early spring, females deposit their adhesive eggs in clusters beneath stones or within crevices. The initial investment per offspring is reflected in the wet weight at birth, where the newly hatched yolk-sac larva emerges at a mass of approximately 0.0018 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0018 grams]. This minuscule starting mass, equivalent to roughly 1.8 milligrams, is a direct consequence of the egg diameter, which ranges between 1.4 and 1.6 millimeters. The larvae are extremely altricial upon hatching, possessing a large yolk sac that sustains them during the first few days of exogenous feeding. This life-history strategy, characterized by the production of numerous small offspring, is typical of many demersal-spawning cottids and reflects a trade-off between egg size and fecundity that shapes population dynamics in variable coastal environments.

Longevity estimates for Taurulus bubalis derive from annual otolith increment analyses conducted on individuals collected from waters with a mean annual temperature of 9.5 °C [T = 9.5 °C]. Under these cool-temperate conditions, the maximum lifespan recorded has been validated at 5 years [am = 5 years], a relatively brief period for a fish of its maximum body size at a temperature of 9.5 °C [T = 9.5 °C]. This lifespan suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early and potentially repeated reproduction over extended somatic persistence. When examined in a comparative context, this longevity is consistent with that reported for other small-bodied coastal sculpins, such as the shorthorn sculpin and the European bullhead, which also exhibit lifespans of between four and six years in similar thermal regimes. The relatively fast pace of life implied by this short maximum age underscores the importance of annual recruitment variability for population stability.

The timing of reproductive events in the Longspined bullhead demonstrates a clear relationship with the thermal environment. Field observations indicate that the spawning period is initiated once water temperatures rise above a seasonal minimum, with the mean annual temperature of 9.5 °C [T = 9.5 °C] serving as a useful benchmark for the general thermal context of the population. Within this thermal framework, the interval between spawning and the emergence of the free-swimming larva is influenced by the ambient temperature during incubation. The yolk-sac larvae, upon hatching at a mass of 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], commence exogenous feeding after the yolk is fully resorbed, a transition that is accelerated at warmer temperatures. Comparative data from related cottids show that the duration of the pelagic larval phase can be substantially shortened by even modest increases in temperature, a pattern that likely holds true for this species and has direct implications for larval dispersal and settlement success in a warming climate.

From a physiological perspective, the size thresholds that define the life cycle of Taurulus bubalis are linked to energetic constraints imposed by the cold-water environment. The ultimate wet weight of 87 grams [Wwi = 87 grams] and the wet weight at puberty of 31 grams [Wwp = 31 grams] represent the endpoints and the midpoint, respectively, of a growth trajectory that is strongly modulated by food availability and temperature. The total length at puberty of 11 centimeters [Lp = 11 centimeters] serves as an important demographic marker, as individuals below this size are reproductively inactive and allocate all available energy toward somatic growth. In contrast, the ultimate total length of 17.5 centimeters [Li = 17.5 centimeters] marks the asymptotic size beyond which growth slows considerably. Maximum longevity in this species, recorded at 5 years [am = 5 years] under a mean thermal regime of 9.5 °C [T = 9.5 °C], indicates that the entire reproductive lifespan is compressed into a relatively narrow window, placing a premium on successful annual spawning events.
